# I Wrote a Brainf*ck JIT Runtime on WASM

The programs we produce have to be executed at some point. How this is done depends on the programming language and its design constraints. I would like to talk about a runtime I wrote for the Brainf*ck programming language.

# What is Brainfuck?
[Brainf*ck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brainfuck) is a programming language created by Urban Müller for the expressed purposed of being extremely minimalistic and thus easy to implement. The execution model of the language maps cleanly to a [Turing machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_machine), where data is read from and written to one cell at a time. The language provides syntax for addressing the next cell to the left or right and even has the notion of input, output and loops! It is simple enough for us to experiment with and reason about different execution strategies.


# Program execution models
As hinted at before, there are different ways to execute a program. The two methods relevant to this post are to compile the source code to something executable or interpret it in place. Compilation is the process of taking some source code in its entirety and outputting some target code via a compiler. For example, you could compile a subset of [JavaScript to C++](https://surma.dev/things/compile-js/), or C to an executable binary (like a .exe on Windows for example). On the other hand, interpretation is the process of translating some source code to a target code on an on-demand basis. That is, the entire program may not be translated until after it begins execution. For example, Python historically has been executed by the PythonC interpreter on a line by line basis with the relevant machine code generated for each line, then executed. The analogy I tend to use is compilation is like translating a book from one language to another where-as interpretation is akin to a speech interpreter translating spoken word in real time.

# Compiled vs Interpreted (pros/cons)
Compilation typically gives you the best performance as the burden of translation and optimisation has already been undertaken by the compiler. Execution can begin immediately and the behaviour of the program is simpler to reason about in the sense that it's easier to understand what the program will do in what sequence. However, compiling any language, even one as simple as Brainf*ck will take time. The larger the program, the longer it will take to compile. We also have to contend with the fact that for every target code we will need to recompile our program. For example, if we want to support both x86 and ARM machine code, we need to compile the program twice, once for each target.

With interpretation, only the interpreter needs to be compiled and we can execute any program we would like. Obviously it becomes harder for us to analyse what the program will do once executed as it is not in its final form until it is being executed. We also have the overhead of translating each step before execution, which drastically slows down the speed of the program compared to a precompiled version.

The execution model used for a programming language implementation must balance startup time, that is, how quickly can we go from source code to execution, and runtime efficiency, i.e. how quickly can we execute each step in an algorithm. I wanted the best of both worlds, and as such I chose a hybrid approach known as Just in Time (or JIT) compilation.
